idiom_name: helper base holding the member, declared before the base that depends on it
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form of the decision: first check whether the language actually fixes base-before-member initialisation. Where it does (C++: virtual bases, then direct bases left to right, then non-static data members), the fix is structural — move the member into a helper base class, declare that base before the dependent base, construct it from the forwarded arguments, and pass the member's value or address to the dependent base's initialiser. Keep the helper private because it is an implementation detail, and give repeated member types a discriminator (a template tag parameter, or a distinct holder type) since a class cannot have two direct bases of one type. Where the language does not fix the order — its base initialiser is an explicit call placed by the programmer — no idiom is needed.
code_sketch:
class DependentBase:                             # needs the member
    construct(value_or_address)                  # bound during construction

class MemberHolder:                              # helper base: initialised first
    member = construct_member(args)

class Derived(MemberHolder, DependentBase):      # base list = load order
    construct(args):
        MemberHolder(args)                       # step 1: the member exists
        DependentBase(member)                    # step 2: base bound to it
pitfalls: Treating the member-initialiser list as the ordering mechanism: bases are initialised in base-specifier order, not in the order that list mentions them, so editing the list changes nothing while editing the base list changes everything.
Skipping the encapsulation: the holder base is an implementation detail, and a public or protected one leaks both the member and the idiom into the class's interface.
Forgetting the discriminator: two direct bases of the same member type are ill-formed, so several members of one type need tags or distinct holder types.

Taking &HolderBase::member instead of this->member when a raw pointer is needed: qualified base-name access yields a pointer-to-member-pointer, not a true pointer — UBSan or ASan may not catch this, leading to silent undefined behaviour.
Inserting a virtual base after the carrier: virtual bases are always initialised first, breaking the ordering guarantee; restructure the hierarchy rather than relying on declaration order.

Assuming the destructor ordering is symmetric: while C++ destroys in reverse construction order (carrier after dependent base), verify the dependent base's destructor does not assume the carrier's member is still alive — std::ostream's destructor does safely flush the streambuf because the streambuf outlives it, but custom bases may not.

Null-pointer literal ambiguity (pre-C++11): NULL is an integer literal; when a constructor overload accepts both a pointer and an integer, passing NULL selects the integer overload — use nullptr (C++11) or an explicit cast to avoid this.

Move operations breaking stored pointers: if the dependent base stores a raw pointer into the carrier's member, a move operation on the derived class leaves that pointer dangling to the donor object's former member.

Wrong move: rely on ASan/UBSan to catch a dependent base constructed from the carrier before the carrier exists -> failure: the base initialiser reads in-bounds but unconstructed storage, which sanitizers routinely miss, so the code passes debug CI and corrupts only in the field -> instead: treat the base-specifier order as a tested contract and add a runtime check that the dependent base observed the carrier's intended value or address.

Wrong move: inherit boost::base_from_member publicly because the forwarding constructors are convenient -> failure: the holder and its member become part of the published interface, and serializers, bindings and ABI checks now see an implementation detail -> instead: inherit privately and reach the member through a typedef or accessor declared inside the derived class.

Wrong move: assume the carrier also orders a virtual dependent base -> failure: the most-derived constructor initialises virtual bases before every direct base, so the carrier lands after the base that needs it and that base still binds unconstructed storage -> instead: restructure so the virtual base receives the value as a constructor argument computed by a static helper, or use two-phase initialisation.
sources: Herb Sutter, GotW #80 'Order, Order!' — definitive coverage of C++ construction/destruction order rules: virtual bases first (depth-first left-to-right), then direct bases in declaration order, then members in declaration order, then constructor body. The canonical reference for why the idiom is necessary and what the exact ordering rules are: https://www.gotw.ca/gotw/080.htm

SEI CERT C++ Coding Standard OOP53-CPP — authoritative secure-coding rule requiring constructor member initializers to be written in canonical order (bases in base-specifier-list order, then members in declaration order) and warning that violating the order is undefined behaviour: https://wiki.sei.cmu.edu/confluence/display/cplusplus/OOP53-CPP.+Write+constructor+member+initializers+in+the+canonical+order
